title: The Great Revolt (66–70 CE)
hookLine: a revolt against Rome ends with Jerusalem and the Temple burned

lines: THROWN OUT IN FRONT OF EVERYONE.
cards: A man in Jerusalem throws a party and tells his servant to invite his friend Kamtza. The servant brings Bar Kamtza instead, a man the host can't stand. The host orders him out.
Bar Kamtza begs: let me stay, I'll pay for what I eat. Half the feast. The whole feast.
No. He is thrown out in front of everyone, and the rabbis at the table say nothing. That's how the Talmud begins its story of the fall of Jerusalem.
Not with armies. With a guest list.

teach.b: The history comes mainly through Josephus, a Jewish commander in the war who later wrote its story under Roman patronage. Judea was ruled by Rome, the governors were harsh, and the people were split among themselves.
Revolt broke out, and Rome sent its legions.

teach.h: THE CITY FIGHTS ITSELF UNDER SIEGE.
teach.b: Inside Jerusalem, rival Jewish factions fought one another even under siege, and Josephus describes the famine inside the walls in harrowing detail.
In the end the Romans broke through, and the Temple, Herod's beautiful house, burned.

teach.h: THE TEMPLE BURNS ON THE NINTH OF AV.
teach.b: The Mishnah, in tractate Taanit, remembers the day: the ninth of Av, the same date tradition gives for the fall of the First Temple. Then the rabbis asked why.
In the Talmud's story, the humiliated Bar Kamtza goes to the Roman authorities and stirs up suspicion against Jerusalem.
When the rabbis might have stopped the plot, one rabbi's overcareful scruples held them back; the Talmud says that rabbi's humility destroyed the house and burned the sanctuary.

teach.h: THE RABBIS ASK WHY: BASELESS HATRED.
teach.b: And in tractate Yoma, the rabbis say the Second Temple was destroyed because of sinat chinam, baseless hatred: people hating one another for nothing. Rome lit the fire, and the rabbis didn't deny it.
But they turned the question inward, toward how people treated each other at the table.
Lamentations, read on the ninth of Av, opens with the grief of an empty city: "How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people!"
The day is still kept with a fast, with mourners sitting low, and with those words read aloud.

how: Jews mark the fall of both Temples on Tisha B'Av, the ninth of Av, with a fast, by sitting low like mourners, and by reading the book of Lamentations.

o: baseless hatred, people hating each other for nothing
the Roman legions that laid siege to the holy city
a vow of silence kept by the rabbis at the feast

games.q: the fall of Jerusalem — tap the pairs.
p: the guest thrown out of the feast
wrote the history of the war

s: the rabbis blamed only Rome for the Temple's fall
Rome burned it, but the rabbis looked inward too: a shaming at a feast, and baseless hatred.
Lamentations is read on the ninth of Av
it opens: "How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people!"
Jerusalem was united against Rome to the end
Josephus describes rival factions fighting each other inside the besieged city.

games.q: you're a rabbi at the feast. the host is throwing Bar Kamtza out in front of everyone. what does the story say you do?
games.why: the rabbis stay silent. Bar Kamtza decides they approved, and goes to stir up Rome against the city. the Talmud makes that silence part of the story of the fall.

practice: Sit low if you can, on a cushion or the floor, the way mourners sit on the ninth of Av, and let one loss come to mind, big or small: a person, a place, a version of your life that ended.
Don't try to fix it or explain it; just let it be in the room with you. If you pray, you can say the line from Lamentations: how doth the city sit solitary.

wordCard.voice: Sinat chinam. Baseless hatred, the sin the rabbis of the Talmud blamed for the Second Temple's fall: hatred between people for nothing.

orig.note: Hebrew: destruction, the word used for the fall of the Temple.

carryVoice: Your line: the second temple fell. The rabbis looked inward, not only at Rome. Day eight hundred ninety-nine, in the books.
